Abstract
Offline preference optimization methods, such
as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), of-
fer significant advantages in aligning Large
Language Models (LLMs) with human values.
However, achieving optimal performance with
these methods typically involves additional hy-
perparameter tuning, resulting in substantial
time overhead. Although prior work has pro-
posed a range of improvements, these meth-
ods remain limited in effectiveness and have
not fully eliminated reliance on hyperparam-
eter tuning. In this work, we propose RMiPO,
a lightweight and efficient framework for of-
fline preference optimization. RMiPO leverages
intrinsic Response-level Mutual information
for Preference Optimization with hyperparam-
eter modulation, dynamically decoupling pref-
erence contributions at negligible additional
computational cost. Extensive experimental
results demonstrate that RMiPO achieves con-
sistently superior performance over existing
methods while reducing training overhead by
more than 15%.
Our code is available at
https://github.com/liavonpenn/rmipo.

Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate re-
markable generation and comprehension capa-
bilities across diverse NLP tasks (Llama, 2025;
DeepSeek, 2025; OpenAI, 2025). However, when
faced with complex tasks such as mathematical
analysis and logical reasoning, LLMs may take
incorrect reasoning paths or generate inconsistent
conclusions. To address this issue, researchers have
proposed Reinforcement Learning from Human
Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022). This ap-
proach fine-tunes pretrained LLMs using carefully
curated human preference data, improving their rea-
soning fidelity and alignment with human values.
Although RLHF substantially enhances LLM
performance, its intricate reward modeling pipeline
and significant computational demands hinder scal-

approaches optimize preferences directly through

Building upon this paradigm, SimPO (Meng et al.,
2024) further eliminates dependence on a reference
model, yielding an approximately 20% reduction
in training time for single-round preference opti-
mization relative to DPO. Empirically, these meth-

pass, RLHF. Nevertheless, as noted in Rasul et al.
(2024), fully realizing their potential still necessi-
tates careful tuning of several key hyperparameters.
This process is nontrivial, as each alignment run
is costly and configuration changes often require
re-establishing optimal hyperparameters.
Recent solutions can be broadly divided into two
types: one embeds dynamic mechanisms in pref-
erence optimization (Wu et al., 2024; Lee et al.,
2025; Wu et al., 2025) to adaptively adjust key
hyperparameters, while the other fundamentally
alters the optimization paradigm, as exemplified
by Xiao et al. (2025b), thereby removing hyper-

parameter dependence. Both approaches exhibit
distinct theoretical and empirical advantages. How-
ever, the former often requires additional monitor-
ing modules or complex control logic, adding extra
training overhead, whereas the latter may degrade
under preference drift or inconsistent data (Yang
et al., 2024; Gorbatovski et al., 2024; Zeng et al.,
2024). This raises a critical research question in
LLM alignment: Is it feasible to develop an effi-
cient method for offline preference optimization?
In this paper, we provide an affirmative answer
to this question. As illustrated in Figure 1, we pro-
pose RMiPO, a lightweight and efficient framework
for offline preference optimization. At its core is
a dynamic modulation mechanism derived from
intrinsic mutual information, enabling RMiPO to
achieve instance-level adaptive tuning of hyperpa-
rameters. Through systematic theoretical analysis,
we find that the hyperparameter γ, which controls
the reward margin, plays a dominant role in prefer-
ence optimization, while the intrinsic mutual infor-
mation of responses provides a principled basis for
its adaptive adjustment. Building on the above in-
sight, RMiPO adaptively adjusts γ during optimiza-
tion, enabling decoupled modeling of preference
contributions at negligible computational overhead.
The primary contributions of this work are as
follows: (1) Lightweight Framework. We pro-
pose RMiPO, a novel lightweight offline preference
optimization framework that leverages intrinsic mu-
tual information to enable instance-level adaptive
hyperparameter control. (2) Insightful Analysis.
We conduct a comprehensive examination of the
roles of hyperparameters in offline preference opti-
mization framework and offer meaningful insights
that can guide future practice and research. (3)
Superior Performance. Through extensive eval-
uations on benchmarks such as AlpacaEval 2 and
MT-Bench, RMiPO reduces training costs by ap-
proximately 15–20% while achieving performance
clearly superior to state-of-the-art baselines.

Methodology
In this section, we address two core design ques-
tions: (1) Which hyperparameters necessitate adap-
tive adjustment, and (2) how to design effective
mechanisms for such adaptation. §3.1 presents two
key insights, and in §3.2 we introduce RMiPO, a
novel offline preference optimization framework
that effectively resolves both of these challenges.
3.1
Motivation and Key Insights
The performance of offline preference optimization
depends on hyperparameter choice, particularly the
trade-off between policy regularization and reward
scaling. Through extensive experiments and theo-
retical analysis, we have distilled two key insights.
Insight I. In offline preference optimization, opti-
mal performance is primarily determined by γ. As
shown in Appendix Table 4, the offline preference
learning paradigm involves more than two hyper-
parameters, but its core remains β, which scales
reward differences, and γ, which controls reward
margins. We fine-tuned Mistral-7B-Base and con-
ducted sensitivity analyses on MT-Bench (Zheng
et al., 2023). Although training curves and in-
domain validation are similar across configurations,
MT-Bench scores vary sharply (Figure 2). In DPO,
except for β = 0.01, which performs relatively

While incorporating γ into DPO yields negligi-

3.2
Proposed Framework: RMiPO
These insights establish two principles: treating
γ as the key adaptive variable and updating it via
mutual information differences. To this end, we
propose RMiPO, a novel optimization framework.
Overview. Figure 4 illustrates the RMiPO train-
ing workflow. Given a prompt x and a preference
pair (yw, yl), the policy model πθ computes point-
wise mutual information for each response, denoted


as PMI(y|x). Unlike the raw log-likelihood dif-
ference, which entangles semantic relevance with
response priors, the PMI difference ∆pmi more
directly disentangles conditional relevance from
marginal popularity. This signal (Step ❸) thus en-
ables reliable and efficient adaptation of the reward
margin γ and offers advantages over prior work.
Details are provided in the following sections.
Objective.
In offline preference optimization,
the policy πθ increases ∆R by maximizing the
log-likelihood ratio between preferred and less-
preferred responses, defining the gradient direc-
tion for preference learning. The reward margin
γ gates updates based on semantic separability:
samples with ∆R > γ are suppressed, others con-
tribute. To this end, RMiPO employs the pointwise
mutual information difference, ∆pmi(x, yw, yl) =
PMI(yw|x)−PMI(yl|x), as an intrinsic metric for
semantic separability. This signal eliminates inter-
ference from non-semantic factors, such as prior
frequencies. Building on this, RMiPO introduces
a key design: the reward margin γ is negatively
correlated with ∆pmi.
Under this mechanism,
semantically distinct pairs (high ∆pmi) receive
smaller margins to promote saturation and reduce
redundancy. Conversely, ambiguous samples (low
∆pmi) retain larger margins to sustain gradients on
semantic differences at the decision boundary.
As shown in Fig. 3, in early training the policy πθ
lacks reliable preference discrimination, resulting
in an effectively ungated margin regime (∆R < γ)
where most samples remain gradient-active. As
learning progresses, the margin γ progressively re-
allocates gradients, yielding a smooth transition
from coarse discrimination to fine-grained align-
ment. To model this nonlinear dependency, we
define the dynamic margin as a rectified exponen-
tial decay of the pointwise mutual information dif-
ference: γ(x, yw, yl) = γmin + (γmax −γmin) ·
exp(−max(0, ∆pmi)).
The rectification intro-
duces asymmetry: when ∆pmi ≤0, the margin is
fixed at γmax, enforcing a strong constraint that con-
tinuously penalizes inverted semantic preferences;
otherwise, the margin decays exponentially with
increasing confidence. This design preserves opti-
mization signals in low- and medium-confidence re-
gions while preventing premature margin collapse.
Moreover, inspired by SimPO (Meng et al.,
2024), we incorporate length normalization into the
reward signal to further stabilize training dynamics.
Notably, as shown in the Appendix Table 5, even in
settings without length normalization, our method
remains effective and consistently improves perfor-
mance. Integrating the above design, the final loss
function of RMiPO, LRMiPO, is formulated as:

Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setups
Following (Xiao et al., 2025b), we perform pref-
erence optimization in two settings (Base and In-
struct) across two model families, namely Llama3-
8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Mistral-7B (Jiang
et al., 2023). In the Base setting, the initial pol-
icy is constructed using the supervised fine-tuning
(SFT) pipeline of Zephyr (Tunstall et al., 2023). In
the Instruct setting, we directly adopt the officially
released instruction-tuned models as the initial pol-
icy, skipping the SFT stage. Subsequently, these
models are further optimized for preferences on
the UltraFeedback dataset (Cui et al., 2024). All
experiments are implemented using the alignment-
handbook (Tunstall et al., 2024) and conducted on
four NVIDIA A800 (80GB) GPUs with batch size
128.
The resulting policy models are evaluated on
multiple authoritative benchmarks, including the
Open LLM Leaderboard v2 (Fourrier et al., 2024;
Gao et al., 2024), AlpacaEval2 (Li et al., 2023), and
MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023). To further assess
safety alignment, we conduct targeted fine-tuning
and evaluation on the Anthropic-HH (Helpful and
Harmless) dataset (Bai et al., 2022).

Experimental Results
Results on instruction-following. As shown in
Table 1, we report the performance of each model
on commonly used instruction-following bench-
marks. All preference optimization methods im-
prove over the initial policy, with RMiPO achiev-

Under the
Llama3-8B-Instruct setting, RMiPO attains 49.1%

5
Related Work
Preference Optimization for LLM. Preference
optimization is a key technique for aligning LLMs
with human values. This paradigm was originally
proposed by (Ouyang et al., 2022) and employs
proximal policy optimization for online training.
However, the high complexity of online algorithms
has driven researchers to shift toward more effi-
cient offline methods. Offline preference optimiza-
tion (Park et al., 2024; Rafailov et al., 2023; Zhao
et al., 2023; Azar et al., 2024; Ethayarajh et al.,
2024; Xu et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024; Amini
et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a,c)
directly leverages paired preference data to guide
policies toward preferred behaviors. Building on
this line of work, (Meng et al., 2024; Hong et al.,
2024) proposed an approach that does not require a
reference model. Despite their effectiveness, these
methods require extensive hyperparameter tuning.
Efficiency Improvement in DPO. Unlike prior
work on data filtering (Muldrew et al., 2024; Yang
et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Corrado et al.,
2025), this study focuses on minimizing hyperpa-
rameter tuning overhead in DPO and its variants.
Existing research has explored several strategies:
(Wu et al., 2024) and (Lee et al., 2025) dynamically
adjust hyperparameters via KL regularization to ac-
count for instance-level preference intensity; (Wu
et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025) introduces an implicit
reference model, reducing hyperparameters that re-
quire tuning; and (Xiao et al., 2025b) proposes
the first parameter-free preference optimization ob-
jective based on perplexity. While these methods
demonstrate success, they remain limited in effec-
tiveness. To address this, we propose RMiPO, an
adaptive hyperparameter tuning mechanism based
on intrinsic mutual information that improves align-
ment while reducing optimization overhead.
6
Conclusion
In this paper, we propose RMiPO, a lightweight and
efficient offline preference optimization framework.
Its core innovation is an adaptive modulation mech-
anism based on intrinsic response-level mutual in-
formation. This mechanism dynamically decou-
ples the contribution of different samples to the
overall preference signal, enabling finer-grained
alignment control.
Theoretical analysis shows
that this mutual information–driven strategy offers
strong interpretability, establishing a new princi-
pled paradigm for sample weighting in preference


optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate
that RMiPO achieves superior alignment gains with
lower training costs and favorable convergence.
Limitations
The core advantage of RMiPO lies in its ability to
obviate the manual tuning of task-sensitive hyper-
parameters, rather than reducing the number of
tunable parameters. This property substantially en-
hances the practicality of preference optimization
algorithms. Nevertheless, RMiPO still exhibits sev-
eral limitations that warrant further investigation.
Sensitivity. While γ is the primary driver of adap-
tivity, its efficacy presupposes that β lies within
a reasonable range, as typically ensured by stan-
dard model-scaling practices. Although extreme β
values destabilize all preference-optimization base-
lines, RMiPO exhibits greater robustness, with per-
formance degrading more gracefully than static-
margin methods. By dynamically adjusting the
reward margin γ (and its bounds) as a function of
β, the proposed exponential decay mechanism par-
tially mitigates mis-scaled preference signals and
reduces performance degradation under suboptimal
settings. Although RMiPO cannot compensate for
arbitrarily ill-chosen β, its adaptive margin con-
sistently offers a safety buffer over fixed-margin
baselines. The coupled dynamics between β and
γ therefore warrant further study in the context of
optimization stability and generalization.
Scalability.
Recent studies suggest increasing
policy optimization iterations can further improve
instruction-following performance. However, due
to computational constraints, this work, like most
existing studies, does not conduct extensive valida-
tion under large-scale regimes. Our experiments
focus on billion-parameter models, which suffice
to elucidate RMiPO’s key mechanisms and provide
empirical support for its effectiveness. The gener-
alization of RMiPO to ten-billion-parameter models
remains to be systematically evaluated.
Adaptability. This work focuses on offline prefer-
ence optimization with fixed datasets, which lim-
its adaptation to dynamic environments. Extend-
ing RMiPO to an online learning framework with
real-time interaction feedback could improve its
applicability to scenarios such as human–computer
interaction and autonomous agents, for example by
using an online oracle to provide preferences and
intrinsic mutual information to guide exploration.
Ethical Considerations
This work proposes a lightweight framework for
LLM alignment. The study does not involve hu-
man participants or personal or sensitive data, nor
does it enable malicious use; therefore, it raises
no ethical concerns. The proposed method aims
to improve the robustness and efficiency of value
alignment, supporting the reliable deployment of
large language models. Furthermore, LLM-based
assistants were employed solely for linguistic re-
finement, with the authors explicitly retaining full
responsibility for the research design, technical
content, and final conclusions.

Revisiting Baseline Methods
This section revisits SOTA baseline methods for
offline preference optimization by examining the
underlying design motivations and the functional
roles of hyperparameters in their loss formulations.
Based on this analysis, we summarize and contrast
the resulting optimization objectives in Table 4.
• DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): By introducing a
difference term of log-likelihood ratios, DPO
implicitly models the reward function, thereby
avoiding reliance on an explicit reward model
in RLHF. This method introduces a tunable
hyperparameter β to control the deviation of
the policy model from the reference model,
enabling a controllable trade-off between pref-
erence alignment and policy updates.
• SLiC (Zhao et al., 2023): The optimization
objective of SLiC incorporates a supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) term and is governed by two
hyperparameters: the margin parameter δ ,
which sets the boundary of the ranking loss,
and the weighting coefficient λ , which bal-
ances the contribution of the SFT term within
the overall objective.
• IPO (Azar et al., 2024): IPO transforms pref-
erence learning into a regression problem with
a squared loss by defining a surrogate reward
function, thereby avoiding the instability as-
sociated with reinforcement learning training.
This approach involves a hyperparameter β
that controls the magnitude of the reward sig-
nal.
• CPO (Xu et al., 2024): CPO directly uses the
log-likelihood as the reward signal and jointly
optimizes it with a SFT term. This method
introduces two hyperparameters: β , which
scales the log-probability term, and λ , which
adjusts the weight of the SFT term in the joint
objective.
• KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024): KTO learns
from unpaired preference data, with its opti-
mization objective governed by three hyper-
parameters: β , which controls the degree of
deviation of the policy model from the refer-
ence model, and λw and λl , which weight
the preference terms corresponding to win-
ning and losing responses, respectively.
• SimPO (Meng et al., 2024): SimPO does not
rely on a reference model and is trained by
optimizing a length-regularized objective over
response pairs, with its objective function gov-
erned by two hyperparameters:
β , which
scales the log-probability term, and γ , which
adjusts the reward margin.

Implementation Details
Dataset: In this work, the training of the policy
model primarily relies on two preference datasets:
UltraFeedback-Binarized (Cui et al., 2024) and
Anthropic-HH (Bai et al., 2022).
• UltraFeedback-Binarized: The original Ul-
traFeedback dataset contains 64,000 prompts,
each with four responses from various open-
and closed-source language models. All re-
sponses are rated by GPT-4 based on overall
quality (overall_score). In the UltraFeedback-
Binarized version, a preference pair is formed
by the highest-scoring response (the “pre-
ferred” response) and one randomly selected
response from the remaining three (the “less-
preferred” response). Policy models trained
on this dataset are evaluated on instruction-
following benchmarks and downstream tasks.
• Anthropic-HH: Anthropic-HH is a human-
labeled dialogue preference dataset compris-
ing two subsets, focusing on “helpfulness”
and “harmlessness.” The dataset originates
from manually constructed and red-teamed di-
alogue samples, designed to study how crowd-
sourced annotators perform red-team attacks
and which strategies are effective. Policy mod-
els trained on Anthropic-HH are primarily
used for safety alignment evaluation.
Training: RMiPO is designed for simplicity and
strong performance, with the full procedure pro-
vided in Algorithm 1. Its core lies in leveraging
response-level PMI for hyperparameter adaptation.
Specifically, πθ(y) denotes the prior popularity of
response y, defined as the joint probability of the
sequence: πθ(y) = Q|y|
t=1 πθ(yt | y<t). Unlike
πθ(y | x), this formulation removes dependence on


the prompt x, enabling explicit decoupling between
response priors and semantic relevance.
For probability estimation, πθ(y) is computed
exactly over the full sequence without trunca-
tion or approximation, ensuring consistency with
information-theoretic definitions.
For datasets
where prompts and responses are concatenated, we
apply a lightweight string-matching heuristic to ex-
tract y. Although this may introduce minor bound-
ary inaccuracies, it preserves intended decoupling.
Consequently, ∆pmi serves as an intrinsic measure
of semantic separability, mitigating bias from non-
semantic factors such as high-frequency tokens.
All models are trained under a unified setup with
β = 2.0, γmin = 0.3, and γmax = 1.6, following
the search space of SimPO. During SFT, we use
a learning rate of 2 × 10−5; across both SFT and
preference optimization, we adopt a batch size of
128, a maximum sequence length of 2048, and train
for one epoch using Adam with cosine annealing.
All experiments are conducted on four 80GB A800
GPUs. Baselines follow the same search protocol
as SimPO: method-specific hyperparameters are de-
tailed in Table 4, and learning rates are tuned within
[3 × 10−7, 1 × 10−6]. In contrast, RMiPO (and Sim-
PER) require tuning only the learning rate, without
introducing additional hyperparameters.
Evaluation: Evaluation on AlpacaEval 2 adopts
the same hyperparameter settings as SimPO: decod-
ing temperatures are set to 0.7 and 0.5 for Mistral-
Base and Mistral-Instruct, respectively, while both
Llama-3 variants use a temperature of 0.9. Evalu-
ation on MT-Bench follows the official decoding
configuration, which specifies task-specific sam-
pling temperatures.
To systematically examine
the impact of preference optimization methods on
downstream task performance, we evaluate mod-
els trained with each method on the standard tasks
included in the Hugging Face Open LLM Leader-
board, strictly following established evaluation pro-
tocols. For safety evaluation, we assess models
trained on the Anthropic HH dataset using its test
set as the benchmark, measuring the probability
that the model generates preferred responses over
less-preferred ones.

Space and Time Complexity Analysis. To evalu-
ate the practicality of RMiPO and baseline methods,
we analyze space consumption (GPU memory) and
time efficiency (computational throughput) under
identical hardware settings, parallelization strate-
gies, and model architectures.
Space complexity. GPU memory during training
is dominated by model parameters, optimizer states,
gradients, and activations. DPO-based methods
(e.g., DPO, β-DPO, ϵ-DPO) require an additional
frozen reference model πref to compute the KL
constraint. Although it does not require optimizer
states, its parameters still occupy substantial mem-
ory, leading to a peak utilization of 82%. In con-
trast, SimPO, SimPER, and RMiPO eliminate the ref-
erence model entirely. As a result, RMiPO reduces
peak memory usage to 62% (an approximately 20%
absolute reduction), enabling larger batch sizes or
longer sequences and mitigating memory and com-
munication bottlenecks in distributed training.
Time complexity. Per-step runtime is determined
by the number of forward and backward passes.
DPO-style methods incur additional latency due to
an extra forward pass through πref, although this
overhead is limited because no gradients are com-
puted. SimPO and SimPER require only a single
forward and backward pass, achieving the highest
efficiency. In contrast, α-DPO introduces complex
dynamic offsets and nonlinear gradient operations,
resulting in the highest per-step latency. RMiPO has
a runtime of O(T) + ∆, where ∆arises from
computing the PMI-based margin term γ(x, yw, yl)
with lightweight logit-level operations. Despite
this small overhead, RMiPO converges faster and
achieves better alignment.
Compared with DPO, which incurs an additional
30%–50% memory overhead, RMiPO maintains a
lower memory footprint via its reference-free de-


sign while introducing only minimal computational
overhead, yielding a favorable trade-off between
efficiency, scalability, and alignment performance.
Mechanism analysis. This section provides ad-
ditional theoretical clarification and empirical vali-
dation for the exponential scheduling mechanism
and constraint bounds adopted in RMiPO. We aim
to further substantiate that these design choices
are grounded in principled considerations rather
than heuristic tuning. Preference optimization is
inherently conducted in the log-probability space.
Therefore, an exponential mapping naturally aligns
with the log-ratio structure of the objective function.
This alignment ensures that the adaptive scaling re-
mains geometrically consistent with the additive
formulation in the log domain. More specifically,
the exponential transformation preserves the rela-
tive ordering of preference signals while enabling
controlled amplification of marginal differences.
Compared with alternative mappings (e.g., linear or
cosine), it provides a more balanced modulation be-
havior: in high-confidence regions, it avoids under-
modulation and preserves discriminative gradients;
in low-confidence regions, it suppresses excessive
scaling and prevents noisy updates. As a result,
the exponential schedule facilitates a smoother and
more stable gradient flow throughout training. The
parameters γmin and γmax are introduced as stabil-
ity constraints rather than task-specific hyperparam-
eters. Their primary role is to restrict the adaptive
scaling within a safe region. These bounds serve
two key purposes: preventing gradient explosion
during early training stages or under noisy PMI es-
timation, and avoiding the dominance of marginal
scaling over the main optimization objective. From
a regularization perspective, the constraint interval
enforces robustness across different random seeds
and model architectures, ensuring consistent con-
vergence behavior.

Abstract: Offline preference optimization methods, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), of- fer significant advantages in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values. However, achieving optimal performance with these methods typically involves additional hy- perparameter tuning, resulting in substantial time overhead. Although prior work has pro- posed a range of improvements, these meth- ods remain limited in effectiveness and have not fully eliminated reliance on hyperparam- eter tuning. In this work, we propose RMiPO, a lightweight and efficient framework for of- fline preference optimization. RMiPO leverages intrinsic Response-level Mutual information for Preference Optimization with hyperparam- eter modulation, dynamically decoupling pref- erence contributions at negligible additional computational cost. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that RMiPO achieves con- sistently superior performance over existing methods while reducing training overhead by more than 15%. Our code is available at https://github.com/liavonpenn/rmipo.
